archive.checked_note: Update #2 finished rolling out on 19 May 2026. This page is a fixed archive built on 21 September 2026 — it is not polled and does not change.
archive.hero_caption: Finished. 5 languages went beyond the Update #1 roster (Burundi Sign Language, Ibinda, Kipende, Papiamento (Aruba), Zapotec (Lachiguiri)); 4 languages that had Update #1 never received this one (Emberá (Northern), Guéré, Turkish Sign Language, Zapotec (del Valle)).
legend: ¶ — the second jw.org created the language’s record, which is when the vernacular was taken in rather than when it became watchable.
archive.method_note: Reconstructed from jw.org after the fact. Each language’s time is the second jw.org created its media record, recovered from the record’s own identifier because the media API overwrites its publish times once an update is complete. The language list itself is read live from the same media service the live tracker uses.
notices: This page is a reconstruction, not a recording. The tracker was not running when Update #2 rolled out, so every time here was recovered afterwards from jw.org rather than observed as it happened. What that means in practice is set out below.

The times are preparation times, not the moments each language became watchable. Each one is when jw.org created that language’s record, which is when the vernacular version was taken in — and materials are normally prepared days ahead of a scheduled release. 275 of the 449 languages were already in hand when the video published, so they became watchable together at the moment marked on the chart, not on the dates shown against them. The remaining 174 arrived afterwards, and for those the two are close.

The times are recovered from a record identifier, because jw.org’s own publish times no longer survive. Once an update is finished the media API replaces each language’s firstPublished with one shared value — 275 of the 449 languages here report an identical time, and re-encoding moves the file timestamps — 161 languages had files rewritten after release. Each record’s identifier encodes the second it was created, which neither of those rewrites touches, and it matches jw.org’s own publish time exactly wherever that time is still intact.

There is only one series, where a live page has two. The tracker normally shows the media files running ahead of the catalogue listing, because it watches them diverge. Both signals finished complete here and both now resolve from the same record, so the gap between them cannot be recovered.
